Observation: NSL-KDD training contains no exact duplicate records, whereas UNSW-NB15 training contains 38.55% exact duplicates when the ID column is excluded.
Interpretation: The two datasets differ substantially in record repetition.
Implication: Duplicate concentration may affect how frequently specific traffic patterns contribute to analysis or downstream model training.
Limitation: The analysis does not establish whether duplicate removal would improve intrusion detection performance.

Observation: NSL-KDD contains 17 attack types appearing only in testing, while UNSW-NB15 has the same nine broad attack categories in both partitions.
Interpretation: The datasets differ in attack-label coverage between training and testing.
Implication: NSL-KDD evaluation includes attack labels absent from training, which may create additional generalization challenges for some detection approaches.
Limitation: Test-only labels do not prove that every associated network behavior is completely novel.

Observation: The attack proportion increases by 10.38 percentage points from training to testing in NSL-KDD, but decreases by 13.00 percentage points in UNSW-NB15.
Interpretation: Both datasets exhibit class-composition changes between their partitions, in opposite directions.
Implication: Evaluation results should be interpreted with awareness of differences in attack prevalence.
Limitation: These proportions do not represent real-world attack prevalence.

Observation: Selected numerical and categorical features exhibit train-test distribution differences. NSL-KDD service has TVD 0.2049, while UNSW-NB15 proto has TVD 0.0677.
Interpretation: The magnitude of distribution differences varies across features and datasets.
Implication: Dataset evaluation should examine individual feature distributions rather than relying only on overall class balance.
Limitation: The analysis does not establish the causes of the observed distribution differences or their effect on model performance.

Observation: NSL-KDD same_srv_rate and diff_srv_rate have Spearman correlation -0.920, while UNSW-NB15 dbytes and dpkts have correlation +0.990.
Interpretation: Some selected network traffic features exhibit strong monotonic relationships.
Implication: Examining feature relationships may help identify overlapping information and guide future feature engineering.
Limitation: High correlation does not establish causation or prove that features are redundant.
